S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
examples: Appears not to be listening, looking elsewhere or spacing out during conversation.
Immediately asks to repeat what was just said or instructed.
Does not respond when name is called or answers only after a long delay.
Misses the content of the conversation, giving unrelated answers or out-of-context reactions.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
examples: Starts homework or projects but fails to complete them, submitting unfinished work or missing deadlines.
When given multi-step instructions, follows only the first few steps and forgets the rest.
Starts cleaning or organizing but switches to another task midway, failing to finish.
Leaves almost completed work reports or paperwork unfinished, neglecting the final steps.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
examples: Continually procrastinates or is reluctant to start writing long reports or complex homework.
Avoids activities that require long periods of concentration, such as reading books or studying.
Passes off tasks that require complex thinking or planning to others.
Gets annoyed or resists when asked to start a task that requires significant mental effort.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
examples: Frequently loses school supplies or office supplies like pens, erasers, and calculators.
Always searching for glasses, cell phones, wallets, or keys because they do not know where they are.
Loses necessary documents or materials at home or in the office and cannot find them.
Cannot remember where they placed an item they were holding just moments ago.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention such as difficulty sustaining focus, disorganization, distractibility, and forgetfulness, without the prominent hyperactive or impulsive behaviors seen in other ADHD presentations. Symptoms must be developmentally inappropriate, present for at least six months, and cause clinically significant impairment in academic, occupational, or social functioning, with onset in childhood even if diagnosis is delayed until adulthood. The course is often chronic, though the way impairment manifests can change across the lifespan as environmental demands shift (e.g., transitions in schooling, job complexity, or caregiving roles). It is distinguished from anxiety and mood disorders by the pervasiveness and early onset of attentional difficulties, and from cognitive disorders by its stability over time and lack of progressive decline.

patient.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Shirley was promoted to oversee a larger service line, which dramatically increased her volume of meetings, strategic reports, and regulatory deadlines. For years she had compensated for long-standing attention difficulties with meticulous color-coded spreadsheets, late-night coffee-fueled work sessions, and over-preparation, but the new role demanded she juggle more simultaneous projects and rapidly switch between EPIC dashboards, budget models, and quality metrics. As her health system pushed through a major electronic record upgrade and COVID-related backlog initiatives, she began missing key follow-ups and struggling to keep track of complex initiatives despite putting in longer hours and tightening her routines at home. The growing gap between her reputation as a highly organized leader and her private sense of falling behind at work, coupled with feedback from colleagues about dropped balls, led her to seek psychiatric evaluation after her primary care doctor suggested her lifelong focus problems might reflect undiagnosed ADHD rather than simply stress or aging.
patient.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to stay focused long enough to get through all the reports and planning tasks my job requires anymore.”

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
S002.manifestation: When I'm in these long strategy meetings or trying to work through a stack of quality reports, I start out focused, but after about ten minutes my mind drifts, I realize I’ve been staring at the same EPIC dashboard without absorbing anything, and I have to reread or re-ask things everyone else seemed to catch the first time.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
S003.manifestation: My team will be giving me a quick rundown in my office and I’ll suddenly realize I’ve missed the middle of what they said, so I’ll have to ask them to repeat the key point or pretend I followed when I really didn’t because my brain just checked out for a moment even though I was looking right at them.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
S004.manifestation: People will email me a list of three or four things they need—like approve a budget change, schedule a follow-up, and send a summary—and I’ll do the first one, maybe start the second, then get pulled into another task and forget the rest until someone gently chases me a week later.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
S006.manifestation: Anything that requires sustained concentration, like drafting a complex service-line plan or reading through a 40-page regulatory update, feels so mentally exhausting that I’ll keep finding excuses to check email, refill my coffee, or jump to easier tasks instead of just sitting down and pushing through it.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
S007.manifestation: Despite all my color-coded folders and systems, I’m constantly misplacing things I need right then—my meeting notebook, my badge, the printout I just highlighted—so I end up wasting ten or fifteen minutes retracing my steps around the office or my house trying to figure out where I absentmindedly set them down.

add_requirements.onset_prior_to_age_12_years: Even back in elementary school, teachers would write on my report cards that I was smart but 'daydreamed' and missed instructions, and my parents had to sit with me at the kitchen table for hours because I’d lose track of what I was supposed to be doing on homework.
add_requirements.functional_impairment: Over the past couple of years, my dropped follow-ups and missed details have led to delayed reports, irritated emails from physicians and finance, and a sense that my credibility as a reliable leader is slipping, even though I’m working longer hours than ever just to keep up.
add_requirements.duration: These focus and follow-through problems have noticeably worsened and been interfering with my ability to manage my expanded role for a little over two years, since shortly after I took on the larger service line and the system upgrade started.
